newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Russia sign five-year uranium deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia sign five-year uranium deal.

text.p: The United States and Russia signed a five-year agreement to speed up deliveries of uranium from dismantled ex-Soviet nuclear warheads to use in American nuclear power plants, United States Enrichment Corp. said on Monday.
Confirming a report in the Washington Post, USEC spokesman Charles Yulish said the deal was signed on Nov. 14.

The 20-year deal for USEC to buy 500 metric tons of bomb-grade uranium from Russian and Ukrainian weapons converted into low-enriched uranium has been in place for two years. By the end of 1996, the government-owned company will have received the equivalent of 18 tons or about 1,000 warheads worth of uranium.

Terms for purchasing the uranium had been renegotiated annually. Under the new plan, Russia is to send USEC the equivalent of 18 tons of bomb-grade uranium in 1997, 24 tons in 1998 and 30 tons per year in 1999, 2000 and 2001 for about $2 billion, accelerating sales by about 50 percent from the original plan.
"What this does is put the contract on a long-term footing," Yulish said. "This secures one-third of the deal ahead of schedule."
The 20-year deal was originally valued at $12 billion, including $8 billion for the enriched uranium and $4 billion for the natural uranium from the conversion process.

Pricing for the natural uranium had been a sticking point in the annual negotiations because the Russians wanted USEC to pay up front for the natural uranium, but the company did not want to because it had no market for the material.
Under legislation passed earlier this year Russia will keep the natural uranium.

"The success of this approach is good for the country, good for USEC's commercial prospects and good for efforts to reduce the threat of nuclear weapons and materials," USEC President William Timbers said.
USEC was to be privatised in 1997. The company has said it plans to seek a buyer and at the same time plans to prepare for a public offering once the White House gives green light.
J.P. Morgan in 1995 estimated the company could be sold for about $1.8 billion to $2 billion.
Clinton administration officials involved in negotiating the agreement were not immediately available for comment.
